Targets from noisy operating conditions, or from regions where the value function has large gradients, then move the estimate less than targets from low-noise regions, so HGPQ learns quickly where the data are reliable without being misled where they are not. For kernel value iteration with per-target variances that are assigned when a target is collected, we prove a high-probability bound on the error of the value estimate, uniform over the explored region. Pooled over five simulated benchmarks, which include a chemical reactor and a bioprocess, HGPQ approaches the best return found by any method in fewer episodes than GP, kernel and deep RL baselines.

articles.title: Anytime-Valid PAC-Bayes Certificates for Adaptive Test-Time Scaling
articles.summary: Test-time scaling systems often choose how much to sample, which prompt to use, and which verifier or aggregation rule to trust after repeatedly inspecting a calibration set. Standard validation…
articles.abstract: Test-time scaling systems often choose how much to sample, which prompt to use, and which verifier or aggregation rule to trust after repeatedly inspecting a calibration set. Standard validation error bars are not valid after this adaptive selection. We model a test-time scaling recipe as a randomized predictor with a random cost and prove a time-uniform PAC-Bayes certificate that holds simultaneously over all calibration times, all posterior mixtures over recipes, and all data-dependent stopping rules. Thus the same event covers the recipe search that precedes deployment, not merely the fixed recipe finally reported. For a finite grid of budgets and verifiers, the penalty is the familiar $\log M/n$, which in the worst case no certificate valid after selection can avoid, while non-uniform priors and localized posterior mixtures can give sharper certificates for structured searches. We specialize the result to self-consistency and show a complementary margin law: plurality voting improves exponentially in the sample budget only on examples where the correct answer is the generator's unique mode; otherwise more compute can provably amplify errors. The same margin analysis yields an oracle water-filling law for compute allocation. A synthetic audit quantifies the optimism caused by adaptive budget selection, and a 192-example GSM8K audit using gpt-4.1-mini generations illustrates risk-cost reporting for a real inference pipeline. At scale, with two models on GSM8K and MATH-500, selected-best error bars fall below the out-of-split GSM8K risk in up to 22.5% of random splits at a nominal 5% while the certificate never does, and on the full GSM8K test split it tightens to 0.109 (held-out risk 0.039). The results give a lightweight, distribution-free way to report risk and compute claims for adaptive inference systems.

articles.title: MiSTiQ: MicroScaling Trellis Quantization for Extreme KV Cache Compression
articles.summary: Modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly support longer contexts and serve more concurrent requests, increasing both sequence lengths and batch sizes. Both trends increase KV-cache size and…
articles.abstract: Modern large language models (LLMs) increasingly support longer contexts and serve more concurrent requests, increasing both sequence lengths and batch sizes. Both trends increase KV-cache size and memory traffic during inference. KV-cache quantization reduces these costs, with recent approaches using codebook-based vector quantization to achieve extremely low bit widths. However, hardware constraints limit codebook size, and most methods reconstruct the cache in higher-precision floating-point formats for attention, limiting the computational benefits of quantization. To address these limitations, we introduce MiSTiQ, a drop-in replacement for codebook-based vector quantizers that combines trellis-coded storage with microscaling (MX) formats for low-precision computation. We combine trellis quantization with beam search to encode the KV cache over large reconstruction spaces without large codebooks. To support MX computation, we derive MX-Hash functions that generate reconstruction values directly in the target MX element format. These functions use the scale-conditioned marginal distribution of block-normalized Gaussian inputs. On Llama3 and Qwen3, MiSTiQ achieves lower WikiText perplexity and higher GSM8K accuracy than the evaluated baselines across several block-scale formats at approximately 1.25 effective bits per element. With NVFP4, it also achieves the highest LongBench average on both models.

articles.title: Open-fMIND: A Large-Scale Open-Access fMRI Corpus for Pretraining Brain Foundation Models
articles.summary: Self-supervised pretraining has transformed language and vision, but its application to functional MRI (fMRI) is constrained by data access. The largest standardized fMRI resources are governed by…
articles.abstract: Self-supervised pretraining has transformed language and vision, but its application to functional MRI (fMRI) is constrained by data access. The largest standardized fMRI resources are governed by data use agreements and dominated by a small number of acquisition protocols, while the thousands of openly licensed datasets on OpenNeuro are individually small, heterogeneously organized, and unprocessed. We present the first release of Open-fMIND, a uniformly preprocessed, openly accessible corpus of parcellated fMRI timeseries from 322 OpenNeuro studies, comprising 11,379 subjects and 45,731 functional runs. Each run is preprocessed with fMRIPrep and parcellated under 52 atlases spanning 14 families, yielding a massive 2.4 million timeseries. Timeseries are released either denoised with our default pipeline (preproc) or as the fMRIPrep output with its confound files (quasiraw), with functional connectivity matrices, per-run provenance and motion metadata. Open-fMIND is intended as a pretraining resource for self-supervised brain representation learning. Pretraining on it yields downstream performance comparable to that obtained with UK Biobank.

articles.title: Teaching Language Models to Adapt Answer Granularity to Their Confidence
articles.summary: When precise details are uncertain, a coarser answer can retain useful information without guessing or abstaining. We investigate whether language models can learn this behavior through…
articles.abstract: When precise details are uncertain, a coarser answer can retain useful information without guessing or abstaining. We investigate whether language models can learn this behavior through model-conditioned supervision derived from consistency across sampled responses and recognition of answers at different granularity levels. We evaluate LFM2.5-1.2B, Ministral~3~3B, Qwen3.5-9B, and Gemma~4~31B on temporal and geographic questions and three generalization datasets. In several in-domain settings, fine-tuning improves the balance of correctness and informativeness beyond coarsening base answers to the best fixed level. Across generalization datasets, all four models produce coarser answers more often at low than high base-model confidence. The three smaller models' answers are also preferred over base responses on held-out relations when correctness and granularity are considered jointly. These findings demonstrate learnable confidence-related granularity adaptation, with benefits varying by model.

articles.title: BoBDeLaN: Bounded-Bandwidth Context Adaptation for Deep Lagrangian Robot Control
articles.summary: Learned physics-based models provide structure for robot control, but uncertain payloads and unmodeled dynamics limit their predictive accuracy. Context-aware Deep Lagrangian Networks enable…
articles.abstract: Learned physics-based models provide structure for robot control, but uncertain payloads and unmodeled dynamics limit their predictive accuracy. Context-aware Deep Lagrangian Networks enable adaptation through a latent context inferred from measurement histories while retaining Lagrangian structure for each fixed context. However, this structure alone does not constrain sensitivity to measurement disturbances. We introduce BoBDeLaN, which combines a contracting, gain-bounded Recurrent Equilibrium Network context encoder with stable linear filtering to shape disturbance sensitivity across frequencies. This architecture guarantees exponential forgetting of the recurrent initialization and admits a finite-horizon, frequency-weighted bound on context perturbations, which extends to residual torque prediction under a Lipschitz continuity assumption on the context-conditioned dynamics model. We evaluate a low-pass realization within model predictive control on simulated and real hardware manipulation tasks, together with frequency-sensitivity analysis on real-robot data. Compared with an LSTM encoder using the same input filter, BoBDeLaN exhibits reduced high-frequency context sensitivity, lower residual torque prediction error, and smoother motion, with less degradation under injected disturbances.

articles.title: FACE: Flow-Guided Angular Channel Estimation Framework for mmWave MIMO Systems
articles.summary: Acquiring accurate channel state information (CSI) is essential for millimeter-wave (mmWave) multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems. However, it remains challenging due to high-dimensional channels,…
articles.abstract: Acquiring accurate channel state information (CSI) is essential for millimeter-wave (mmWave) multi-input multi-output (MIMO) systems. However, it remains challenging due to high-dimensional channels, limited pilot observations, and measurement noise. To address these challenges, we propose flow-guided angular channel estimation (FACE), a novel channel estimation framework based on flow matching, an emerging generative modeling paradigm that learns continuous transport dynamics between probability distributions. FACE exploits the inherent angular-domain sparsity of mmWave channels and incorporates the learned flow matching model as a generative channel prior. Numerical results show that FACE consistently achieves higher channel estimation accuracy than both conventional estimators and diffusion-based generative estimator across diverse channel and system configurations. Moreover, FACE maintains high estimation accuracy with fewer pilot observations and achieves an average achievable rate close to the perfect-CSI benchmark. Compared with diffusion-based estimation, FACE requires substantially fewer sampling steps while achieving superior or comparable estimation accuracy, reducing inference time and computational cost. Overall, the proposed framework demonstrates the potential of flow matching for accurate, pilot-efficient, and computationally efficient mmWave MIMO channel estimation.

articles.title: Decision-Relevant Forecast Calibration for Predictive Control
articles.summary: Calibration evidence for a predictive controller need not remain valid when operating-context frequencies change. We develop an audit and certification procedure for a declared family of…
articles.abstract: Calibration evidence for a predictive controller need not remain valid when operating-context frequencies change. We develop an audit and certification procedure for a declared family of context-density shifts, with a frozen predictor/controller and unchanged conditional outcome law. Coverage requires calibrated tests to span density-weighted selected-plan sensitivities. A residual Gram matrix yields the minimum augmentation rank and an optimal test budget for uncovered $L_2$ geometry. This optimum need not minimize bias over probability-feasible conditional means. For finite contexts, an asymmetric absolute-loss dual and directional linear programs enclose the continuous worst-shift feasible bias. Intersecting simultaneous moment intervals with the conditional-mean domain gives a further certificate and a linear program for selecting an operating shift after validation. In a designed 240-context study, two spectral directions remove at least 80.8% of the feasible worst-case bias. For a separate misspecified logistic forecaster, matched sensitivity and generic corrections reduce expected cost by 2.590% and 3.239%, with the generic method winning all 200 refits. On 100,000 new episodes, both corrections certify absolute evaluation bias below the illustrative tolerance 0.04 throughout a declared shift interval, while the base certifies no shift. This outcome is highly predictable under the known synthetic law used for design. The probability-feasible certificate does not improve on the moment rectangle in this sample. The contribution is reusable evaluation and audit capability with explicit geometric and statistical limits, rather than recalibration superiority. Evidence uses synthetic finite contexts, known frequencies and committed plans; evaluation bias, oracle regret, constraint risk and feedback deployment remain distinct.

articles.title: Determining Concentration from Raman Spectroscopy with Manifold Learning and Y-shaped Conformal Autoencoders
articles.summary: Monitoring of chemical processes is crucial in chemical engineering, motivating sophisticated process analytical technology (PAT). In-line analytics are advantageous, with Raman spectroscopy being an…
articles.abstract: Monitoring of chemical processes is crucial in chemical engineering, motivating sophisticated process analytical technology (PAT). In-line analytics are advantageous, with Raman spectroscopy being an established and reliable tool in various applications, from which many properties can be determined. We recently [Koronaki et al., AIChEJ 2024] proposed determining polymer particle size from Raman spectroscopic data, by combining Diffusion Maps (a manifold learning method) with a Y-shaped Conformal Autoencoder Neural Network. Herein, we extend this workflow to predict liquid concentrations, allowing also for multiple target predictions from the same model. We apply the methods on two datasets consisting of Raman measurements and concentration measurements: one from microgel polymerization and one from citric acid dissociation. The single-target concentration prediction results, where one target is determined from each model at a time, are accurate. Comparing against dedicated methods such as Indirect Hard Modeling (IHM) is not straightforward, due to the different validation strategies and the considered spectra range; nevertheless, it is fair to say that IHM performs slightly better than the proposed workflow. We further compare this approach with other regression methods, such as artificial neural networks, extreme gradient boosting and partial least squares, and the results show that the Conformal Autoencoders achieve higher predictive performance, demonstrating that the workflow can also be used for concentration determination. Finally we find that single-target concentration predictions are more accurate than the multiple target predictions for both case studies.

articles.title: Locally Linear Generalized Single Index Regression
articles.summary: In this work we propose and analyze a procedure for estimating a generalized single-index regression model. This generalized single-index regression framework models the conditional mean of the…
articles.abstract: In this work we propose and analyze a procedure for estimating a generalized single-index regression model. This generalized single-index regression framework models the conditional mean of the responses $Y$ as a function of the covariates $X$ where the mapping is assumed to have the form $f \circ g$, where $g$ is $β$-Hölder with $β\geq 2$ and $f$ can be a discontinuous function of bounded variation. We propose a general procedure that operates under minimal assumptions about the distribution of covariates $X$, requiring only boundedness, sufficient smoothness and absolute continuity with respect to Lebesgue. Our procedure jointly estimates the gradient vector $\hat v(x) \approx \nabla g(x)$ and the conditional mean $μ(x) = f(g(x))$ by solving a localized weighted linear least squares problem. We derive central limit theorems for gradient vector estimates $\hat{v}_x$ and regression estimates $\hatμ(x)$, and we derive rates of convergence for our approach, illustrating that it indeed achieves a stochastic convergence rate matching the minimax mean squared error rate when $β= 2$ and $f$ has a locally Lipschitz derivative. Unlike prior approaches our velocity estimation results accommodate link functions in the local bounded-variation class, allowing for nonsmooth and even discontinuous links while retaining consistency and asymptotic normality at almost every inference point. Finally, we instantiate this model in the situation where $g = Π$ is a closest point projection onto a compact and regular embedded $C^3$ curve $γ$, a setting recently studied in the literature. We also supplement our theoretical results with experiments on real and synthetic data to demonstrate the utility of our procedure.

articles.title: DEFTS: Data-Efficient, Training-Free Few-Shot Learning for CLIP in the Text Subspace
articles.summary: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) achieves impressive zero-shot image classification performance by comparing image embeddings against class-specific text embeddings. While recent…
articles.abstract: Contrastive Language-Image Pre-training (CLIP) achieves impressive zero-shot image classification performance by comparing image embeddings against class-specific text embeddings. While recent few-shot methods leverage labeled training samples to improve upon this zero-shot baseline, they often predominantly rely on image embeddings and underutilize the semantic structure of the text embeddings. In this paper, we introduce DEFTS, a data-efficient, training-free few-shot classification method strictly in the text subspace. We first demonstrate empirically that while raw text embeddings can be suboptimal as direct classifiers, the linear subspace they span remains highly discriminative. DEFTS therefore proposes to reduce the image-text modality gap by projecting estimated image prototypes directly into this subspace. Importantly, by expressing these prototypes as linear combinations of text embeddings, DEFTS reduces a high-dimensional estimation problem to the derivation of just a few coefficients. These coefficients are then computed via a Bayesian posterior mean, using a prior naturally centered on the original text embedding coordinates. Extensive experiments across 12 image classification benchmarks demonstrate that DEFTS significantly improves upon existing training-free methods.

articles.title: Nonparametric Instrumental Kernel Regression: The Well- and Misspecified Setting Under General Link Conditions
articles.summary: We study nonparametric instrumental variable regression when the outcome takes values in a separable Hilbert space $\mathbb{Y}$, for instance a curve, a density or the kernel mean embedding of a…
articles.abstract: We study nonparametric instrumental variable regression when the outcome takes values in a separable Hilbert space $\mathbb{Y}$, for instance a curve, a density or the kernel mean embedding of a distribution. The structural function solves an ill-posed operator equation whose conditional expectation operator need not be injective, and whose solutions need not belong to the hypothesis space. We analyse a two-stage kernel estimator that extends kernel instrumental variable regression to $\mathbb{Y}$-valued outcomes and allows spectral regularisation in both stages, including Landweber iteration and Showalter's method in the second stage. We show that the second stage is a regularisation method in the Hilbert scale generated by the inverse of the kernel integral operator. This viewpoint identifies the solution towards which the estimator converges: the minimum-norm solution in the reproducing kernel Hilbert space in the well-specified case and, in the misspecified case, the unique solution in the range of the continuous extension of the projection operator associated to the well-specified setting. Under source conditions and link conditions expressed through general index functions, we derive non-asymptotic bounds in a scale of interpolation norms that hold with high probability in terms of the first-stage error, with or without identification and in the well- and misspecified settings. For polynomial link conditions, we recover the rate of scalar kernel instrumental regression and extend it to targets outside the hypothesis space; for exponential link conditions, we obtain logarithmic rates in the severely ill-posed regime.

articles.title: Variance-adaptive confidence regions for fixed-benchmark binomial mixtures, with application to LLM evaluation
articles.summary: We construct confidence intervals for linear functionals $θ(F_m)=\int h\,dF_m$ of the empirical law $F_m$ of success probabilities $p_1,\dots,p_m$, from independent counts…
articles.abstract: We construct confidence intervals for linear functionals $θ(F_m)=\int h\,dF_m$ of the empirical law $F_m$ of success probabilities $p_1,\dots,p_m$, from independent counts $c_i\sim\mathrm{Bin}(n,p_i)$, as for a language model run $n$ times per problem. Coverage is at least $1-α$ for every $n$, $m$ and fixed $(p_i)$, simultaneously for all bounded $h$. The variance-adaptive (VA) region tests each candidate mixing law with the conditional variance of the tail counts it implies. This variance is linear in the law, so the region is a linear program, and cell envelopes keep it valid off-grid. Regions calibrated for iid sampling target a super-population law and are conservative for $θ(F_m)$. With all $n$ tail counts, fixed $n$, continuous $h$ and a grid refined as $m\to\infty$, the identification part of VA's width is first-order worst-case optimal, as for any localization with the same index set. Under a rule fixed before the main comparator runs, VA was narrower than a two-stage plug-in band at every $n$ (median width ratio 0.60 at $n=128$), but not than the asymptotic, pointwise AMARI interval at $n=128$; on real rollout pools it was wider than both pointwise and Bonferroni-adjusted AMARI at $n\le128$. For $P(p>0)$ and pass@$k$ with $k\gg n$ the data support only lower bounds.

articles.title: Dimension-free spectral laws and the risk of spectral filters
articles.summary: Spectral properties of the sample covariance are key to modern machine learning with high-dimensional data. Random matrix theory (RMT) supplies powerful tools; however, most classical results assume…
articles.abstract: Spectral properties of the sample covariance are key to modern machine learning with high-dimensional data. Random matrix theory (RMT) supplies powerful tools; however, most classical results assume proportional asymptotics, where $d/n$ tends to a finite limit. In functional data analysis and kernel methods, a fixed infinite-dimensional Hilbert space is often the more natural setting for the observations, beyond the scope of proportional asymptotics. This calls for a dimension-free spectral theory for i.i.d. observations $\boldsymbol{x}_1, \dots, \boldsymbol{x}_n$ in a Hilbert space $\mathcal{H}$ with trace-class population covariance $Σ$. Building on the dimension-free ridge regression analysis of Cheng and Montanari (2024), we establish two deterministic equivalents with explicit nonasymptotic error bounds. The first approximates the empirical spectral law $\widehatμ_n$ of the sample Gram matrix by a deterministic law $μ_n$. The second characterizes the conditional prediction risk of analytic spectral filters in linear regression. Previous sharp approximations to prediction risk in this setting have focused on ridge regression and closely-related problems. Our analysis covers a broader class of filters at the bulk scale, with an explicit user-friendly spectral stability condition to check. We apply our theory to power and critical spectral laws, and we recover the proportional regime. For prediction, we study (negative) ridge estimators, iterated ridge, and gradient flow. Mathematically, building on the idea of stochastic interpolation, we construct a deterministic backward path to interpolate the spectral parameter. The resulting bounds on resolvent and mixed-resolvent traces give mesoscopic approximations to the spectral law within the bulk and, by Cauchy's formula, deterministic equivalents for the prediction variance and squared bias of analytic spectral filters.

articles.title: Summary Sufficiency in Simulation-Based Inference via Mutual Information
articles.summary: Simulation-based inference (SBI) enables posterior estimation when the likelihood is intractable but data can be simulated from the model. For high-dimensional or variable-length data, SBI methods…
articles.abstract: Simulation-based inference (SBI) enables posterior estimation when the likelihood is intractable but data can be simulated from the model. For high-dimensional or variable-length data, SBI methods typically rely on low-dimensional summary statistics as conditioning inputs for posterior estimation, making their sufficiency crucial for accurate inference. Mutual information (MI) provides a natural information-theoretic characterization of sufficiency, quantifying how much parameter information a summary retains. However, these MI quantities are generally intractable in likelihood-free settings. Sui et al. (2026) estimate MI from a trained neural posterior using the Barber--Agakov (BA) lower bound, while discussing, but not computing, a Fisher-information upper bound. This makes the estimate ambiguous: a small lower bound may indicate either an insufficient summary or an inaccurate density estimator. We address this limitation with a tractable diagnostic that estimates the BA gap and reveals what the difference between bounds has actually measured. We extend the resulting sufficiency metric to observation-centered restricted data spaces, allowing simulations to focus on a neighborhood of the data while preserving the target posterior and enabling valid sufficiency comparisons between summaries. We illustrate the use of this diagnostic tool on a temporal epidemic-type aftershock sequence model by comparing learned and hand-crafted summary statistics for variable-length earthquake catalogs.

articles.title: The Limits of Closed-Form Couplings for Few-Step Generation
articles.summary: Few-step generators via flow models require complicated technical solutions such as a pretrained flow model or a consistency loss. While rectified flows have gained popularity for their success in…
articles.abstract: Few-step generators via flow models require complicated technical solutions such as a pretrained flow model or a consistency loss. While rectified flows have gained popularity for their success in few-step sampling, they pay a cost of needing a pre-trained model and sampling a large number of couplings per dataset. Yet for a finite dataset and a Gaussian probability path, the probability-flow vector field of the empirical distribution is available in closed form, so one could use this field as the teacher and skip pretraining altogether. We demonstrate that, surprisingly, this approach is impossible for problems of practical relevance. In particular, the analytic solution of the diffusion process in high dimensions becomes almost a linear transformation. The integration returns the noise vector drawn at initialisation, plus a drift that is empirically a faint copy of the data point, almost independent of the noise. The coupling therefore differs from an independent pairing only through this drift. As a result, training a model on these couplings is almost equivalent to training the model on the independent draws of the noise and the data, which does not provide a useful teacher. We highlight that this is the direct consequence of the high-dimensionality of the data, and that for low enough dimensions or large enough datasets, analytic couplings become more efficient teachers. We quantify this effect by the fraction of endpoint energy carried by the drift, which scales as $\frac{\log N}{d}$ for a dataset of size $N$ in a $d$-dimensional space. Finally, we provide an empirical study confirming all the theoretical results presented in the paper.

articles.title: CONGA: Compiling Gaussian Fiber Geometry for Structured Bayesian Inference
articles.summary: In structured Bayesian models, a large latent block is often Gaussian conditional on a smaller set of parameters, yet generic inference methods relearn this geometry during warmup. We study how this…
articles.abstract: In structured Bayesian models, a large latent block is often Gaussian conditional on a smaller set of parameters, yet generic inference methods relearn this geometry during warmup. We study how this structure can be used to construct transports for posterior inference. The conditional mean and precision determine exact affine maps, including symmetric Brenier and triangular Knothe-Rosenblatt maps, that separate a standard normal block from the remaining non-Gaussian core. KL and relative Fisher objectives then reduce to objectives on this core. We introduce CONGA, a compiler that identifies candidate Gaussian blocks and selects a temporal, spectral, or sparse implementation according to their structure and computational cost. Marginalization requires an identity established from the model; numerical evidence alone permits only a target-preserving change of variables, and a failed check leaves the model unchanged. On the Stock-Watson inflation model, CONGA improves minimum ESS per second by 12.5x for NUTS. It also restores convergence where the raw target fails: for WALNUTS on the same model, and for NUTS on a 6760-dimensional electricity load model reduced to 34 core coordinates. Experiments on graph-indexed fields show how coloring and fill affect the choice of map, including cases where retaining the original target is preferable. Code at https://github.com/vicgalle/conga

articles.title: FARCH: A Functional ARCH Model for Calibrated Prediction Bands
articles.summary: Forecasting a curve, rather than a handful of scalar summaries of it, requires a notion of uncertainty that is itself functional. We propose FARCH, a functional nonlinear autoregressive model with…
articles.abstract: Forecasting a curve, rather than a handful of scalar summaries of it, requires a notion of uncertainty that is itself functional. We propose FARCH, a functional nonlinear autoregressive model with conditional heteroscedasticity, in which the conditional mean and the conditional volatility of the next curve are forecasted jointly and nonparametrically, by reusing a single kernel weighting scheme --- built on a wavelet semi-metric between curves --- first on the curves themselves and then on their squared residuals. From this pair of estimators we derive two constructions of prediction bands: a pointwise band, obtained from marginal scenario quantiles, and a uniform, sup-norm band, calibrated for decisions that concern the entire forecasted path rather than any single instant. Applied to day-ahead forecasting of half-hourly French national electricity demand (1996--2009), and compared, under an identical protocol, against four existing prediction-interval constructions that do not model the conditional variance explicitly, the uniform FARCH band attains pointwise coverage statistically indistinguishable from its nominal target at the 80%, 90% and 95% levels, and a curve-wise coverage of 90.1%, significantly above the 70.8% reached by the best competing method, at the cost of a wider interval. Pointwise bands, in contrast, undercover regardless of whether the variance is modelled explicitly, indicating that state-dependent volatility and simultaneous calibration are two distinct ingredients that a trustworthy prediction band must combine.

articles.title: A Convergence Analysis of the Random Feature Method for Linear PDEs
articles.summary: The Random Feature Method (RFM) distinguishes itself among machine learning approaches to partial differential equations (PDEs) through its superior accuracy and computational efficiency.…
articles.abstract: The Random Feature Method (RFM) distinguishes itself among machine learning approaches to partial differential equations (PDEs) through its superior accuracy and computational efficiency. Nevertheless, the theoretical underpinnings of RFM remain incompletely elucidated. This paper provides a comprehensive analysis of RFM within the framework of kernel methods, focusing on two principal aspects: (i) approximation by finitely many random features in Sobolev norms and the PDE residual seminorm, and (ii) estimation over the induced reproducing kernel Hilbert space (RKHS) from finitely many noiseless collocation observations. We relate both problems to kernel ridge regression (KRR) and establish upper and lower bounds in terms of the eigenvalues of the associated integral operators under the respective assumptions. Combining the approximation and estimation lower bounds, we establish a lower bound under simultaneous restrictions on the numbers of random features and collocation observations. We further quantify how activation regularity affects these eigenvalues, obtaining algebraic upper bounds for finitely smooth activations and stretched-exponential upper bounds for analytic activations.

articles.title: Enhancing Mixed Oil Length Prediction through Graph Representation Learning
articles.summary: During the pipeline transportation of refined oil products, the inevitable formation of mixed oil segments poses considerable economic challenges to pipeline networks. Therefore, it is important to…
articles.abstract: During the pipeline transportation of refined oil products, the inevitable formation of mixed oil segments poses considerable economic challenges to pipeline networks. Therefore, it is important to accurately predict the length of these mixed oil segments. Although previous methods have achieved relatively accurate predictions by integrating machine and deep learning algorithms, they ignore the statistical dependencies that remain among real-world mixed oil samples, which degrades model accuracy. To address this issue, we propose a novel Sample Dependencies Incorporated Graph Representation Learning (SDI-GRL) model. By representing samples and pipeline features as nodes of a graph, SDI-GRL connects dependent samples through their shared features, allowing message passing to propagate information across related samples. This graph-based framework allows our model to capture the statistical dependencies among samples absent in prior works. A case study on a mixed oil dataset demonstrates that our SDI-GRL model surpasses the strongest existing approach, reducing both the RMSE and the MAE by more than 10%.

articles.title: Calibrated Functional Prediction from Overlapping Nonlinear Observations
articles.summary: We study prediction of nonlinear audit functionals from scalar observations of a shared hidden table state. For Schur-rational operators, local Gaussian projections yield a common sparse kernel for…
articles.abstract: We study prediction of nonlinear audit functionals from scalar observations of a shared hidden table state. For Schur-rational operators, local Gaussian projections yield a common sparse kernel for overlapping tasks, repeated row identities, and cross-row dependence. Shared-state residual samples extend this kernel through a positive-semidefinite feature representation. Positive matrix integration and sample-value enclosures connect the original inputs to the actual saved hybrid prediction. A sorted calibration-role perturbation bound then certifies its complete finite-pool pinball risk. Independent complete-loss selection chooses the ridge, score scale, and residual weight, while task-rank calibration supplies an upper endpoint. Evaluation uses twenty new reference contexts per dataset at two task sizes, giving 400 conditions across ten benchmark populations. The mean dataset complete-loss ratios are 0.9977 to the degree-two kernel, 0.9961 to matched complete-MC shrinkage, and 0.9911 to the retrospective minimum over 174 public configurations. The last ratio has a paired reference-bootstrap interval of [0.9898,0.9927]. On 40 profiles at coefficient tolerance $10^{-7}$, Gamma quadrature has a geometric mean cold-time ratio of .0646 to strengthened Arb/Petras integration.

articles.title: Decorrelation Before Variable Selection: Left and Right Transforms and Their Trade-Off
articles.summary: Decorrelation has two forms. A left transform keeps coefficients and changes noise; a right transform keeps noise and changes coefficients.
articles.abstract: Decorrelation has two forms. A left transform keeps coefficients and changes noise; a right transform keeps noise and changes coefficients. Cholesky whitening alone keeps noise variables inactive when true ones come first; decorrelation preserving coefficients and noise loses information.

articles.title: High-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses
articles.summary: In this work, we study high-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses, allowing different domain-specific regression coefficients, cumulative links and thresholds. We develop the…
articles.abstract: In this work, we study high-dimensional transfer learning with unaligned ordinal responses, allowing different domain-specific regression coefficients, cumulative links and thresholds. We develop the sample-split and full-target algorithms that pool source and target likelihoods and then estimate a target correction. Under suitable conditions, our algorithms achieve minimax-optimal rates for parameter estimation and excess risk. Simulations favor the full-target algorithm over the sample-split algorithm for finite-sample estimation and prediction. An application to a medical dataset further demonstrates the predictive gains of our full-target algorithm over the target-only and pooled baselines when transferring information from the five-category source data to binary hospital mortality.

articles.title: Generalized Prediction Set with Bandit Feedback
articles.summary: In high-stakes environments where uncertainties abound, set-valued prediction offers a cautious and robust mechanism by presenting multiple potential labels as the prediction for each test instance…
articles.abstract: In high-stakes environments where uncertainties abound, set-valued prediction offers a cautious and robust mechanism by presenting multiple potential labels as the prediction for each test instance to mitigate the potential risk associated with prediction errors. Yet, integrating this paradigm with out-of-distribution (OOD) detection remains scarcely explored in such settings as online learning with bandit feedback. The bandit feedback mechanism informs the learner about the correctness of the pulled arm/action instead of the explicit ground truth label, leaving the true class label unknown when an incorrect action is taken. To address this challenge, we introduce BanditGPS which conducts set-valued prediction with OOD detection in the bandit feedback setting, using an estimation to the ground truth of class labels. BanditGPS achieves three objectives: render small/informative prediction sets, enhance the OOD detection performance, and control the recall for all normal classes to meet prescribed requirements. Our approach is characterized by the loss function, which trades off between high OOD detection and small prediction sets. Theoretically, we prove that the convergence rate of the regret is $\tilde{\mathcal{O}}(T^{-1/2})$. The empirical results further show that BanditGPS effectively controls the recalls with promising performances on OOD detection and informative prediction.

articles.title: DiagTrace: An Interactive Benchmark for Clinical Decision Making
articles.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning benchmarks. However, existing evaluations typically provide all patient information…
articles.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have shown strong performance on medical question answering and diagnostic reasoning benchmarks. However, existing evaluations typically provide all patient information upfront and assess only the final diagnosis or rationale. This setup ignores the need to acquire diagnostic evidence incrementally from incomplete information in real-world diagnosis. To bridge this gap, we introduce DiagTrace, a source-grounded benchmark for evaluating whether LLMs can reconstruct the documented diagnostic trajectory through interactive information seeking. Each benchmark instance is built from a PubMed Central case report and includes an initial presentation, an event bank, a clinical course, and diagnostic references. DiagTrace contains 510 cases across eight specialties, with 225 used to evaluate four LLMs on clinical-course alignment, interaction quality, and efficiency. Results reveal trade-offs in coverage, source-consistent ordering, and turn use.

articles.title: KV-LTM: Persistent Per-Session KV Caches as Long-Term Memory for Personal Assistants
articles.summary: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on…
articles.abstract: Personal assistants accumulate months of conversations, but today's long-term memory stacks put derivation or selection between a question and its evidence. In a system-level comparison on LongMemEval, two commercial assistants scored well below the same model reading the history offline [1], consistent with, but not isolating, content loss between write and read. We propose KV-LTM: a memory tier storing each session's raw text plus its KV cache under a fixed reader model, answering by restoring cached sessions and appending the question. KV-LTM is complementary to, not a replacement for, retrieval and indexing. Text is the memory of record; the cache is a recompute-free prefill accelerator, degrading gracefully to text. We specify the design: storage record, budget-derived retention, append-only read path, and bounded aggregation. We size it analytically: across pinned BF16 full-attention (GQA) and latent-cached MLA configurations, per-token state spans approximately 31K-328K bytes (the pinned KDA+MLA hybrid differs: approximately 8.1K bytes/token plus a fixed per-session recurrent term), giving approximately 0.34-3.6 TB per user-year at a declared 30K-token/day scenario, against approximately 49 MB of raw text; per-query cost is modelled as regime-conditional transfer, attention, decode, aggregation, and compute. We define an evaluation protocol needing no persistent-cache implementation for logical QA evaluation: per-session prefill emulates valid cache reuse under the same model/input-state contract and ideal arithmetic, with named arms, controlled baselines, and a preregistered reader-model gate; a separate minimal real-cache replay tests numerical equivalence and measures the cost axis, with outcomes not assumed. KV-LTM trades storage for avoided re-prefill compute and write-time fidelity, within a declared retention budget.

articles.title: WebAgents: Unbundling Agent Creation, Hosting, and Execution for an Agent-Native Web
articles.summary: Large language models are moving from isolated assistants toward autonomous agents that can plan, use tools, and coordinate with others, motivating an emerging Agentic Web of independently developed…
articles.abstract: Large language models are moving from isolated assistants toward autonomous agents that can plan, use tools, and coordinate with others, motivating an emerging Agentic Web of independently developed agents and services. Realizing this vision requires agent behavior to move across creators, hosts, and runtimes without coupling publication to a particular execution environment or transferring authority over user resources. We introduce WebAgents, which unbundles these roles through a signed agent.pkg that carries portable workflows, skills, schemas, and resource requirements. An OpenClaw-based agent-native browser/runtime verifies the package, obtains authorization, and binds it at run time to user-controlled models, tools, permissions, and budgets, while hosts distribute the public program and may retain private services server-side. We demonstrate this contract with three unrelated workflows executed unchanged under local and API-backed models, including literature review with live services and a website-published travel agent using semantic tools and user-selected personal resources. In a controlled suite, WebAgents explicitly blocks all 716 injected contract violations while accepting all 295 matched benign controls, with median automated pre-execution processing below 0.5 s for all three packages. We conclude by outlining a path toward NANDA-based discovery and interoperable package ecosystems while retaining execution authority in the user's runtime.

articles.title: Pathology Randomization for Synthetic Priors and Zero-Shot Detection
articles.summary: Hospital brain imaging archives hold a diverse array of pathology at sample sizes beyond prospective studies, particularly for underrepresented populations and diseases. To unlock uncurated clinical…
articles.abstract: Hospital brain imaging archives hold a diverse array of pathology at sample sizes beyond prospective studies, particularly for underrepresented populations and diseases. To unlock uncurated clinical data and scale analysis, methods are needed to detect abnormalities across contrasts and resolutions. Synthetic data has provided robust, contrast-agnostic models for a variety of human neuroimaging tasks in healthy anatomy, but pathology detection and other tasks in clinical settings still require real patient data, contrast-specific models, or disease-specific generators. We propose PathoDraw, a generative model of brain MRI with pathology. A conditional distribution of lesions given the healthy anatomy is drawn into the label map before contrast-agnostic rendering, and a single network estimates healthy anatomy with exact signed intensity deviation of any input scan. The contrast-agnostic 3D UNet learns the healthy labels under the lesion and the signed deviation directly and identifies pathology via robust tissue statistics and learned features, despite no training on real pathology. We show zero-shot detection on public stroke, tumor, and white matter hyperintensity datasets as well as archived clinical data, spanning $T_1$w, FLAIR and $T_2$w at various resolutions under a recent unsupervised anomaly detection benchmark protocol. Our single model exceeds or performs comparably to contrast-specific anomaly detectors trained on real scans and keeps healthy anatomy intact. The same generator trains networks for super-resolution and for registration in the presence of pathology. Our model, robust across acquisition and disease, enables the use of uncurated, archived data for clinical analysis. Our code is available at https://github.com/agr78/Pathology-Randomizer.

articles.title: Eight in Ten LLMs Leak System-Prompt Secrets: Nevan, an Agentic Capture-the-Flag Study
articles.summary: We audit instruction-hierarchy enforcement across 363 text-in/text-out models from the OpenRouter catalog. The research question we answer with this experiment is which models disclose a protected…
articles.abstract: We audit instruction-hierarchy enforcement across 363 text-in/text-out models from the OpenRouter catalog. The research question we answer with this experiment is which models disclose a protected secret embedded in the system prompt, and through which techniques. Each model guards a secret 16-character flag set in its system prompt, while an artificial intelligence (AI) agent (OpenCode, powered by DeepSeek V4.1 Flash), steered by a human researcher, tries to persuade it to emit the flag. The flag was exfiltrated from 296 of the 363 models, plus four models released after the initial catalog freeze, for 300 captures in total. Of these, 170 involved a non-English language pivot, most often French. Each capture shows that a model ranked a user request above its system instruction at least once. It does not show that the model provably resists untested attacks, nor that it would consistently leak semantically sensitive data, nor that it is vulnerable to harmful-content jailbreaks. For practitioners, we draw three lessons: do not store secrets in system prompts, enforce critical behavior outside the model with output validation and deterministic checks, and do not let a large language model (LLM) judge be the sole decider of consequential outcomes.

articles.title: DiscoveryAgent: A Framework for Scientist-centric Agentic AI
articles.summary: AI agents can assist scientific research, but balancing autonomous investigation with scientists' ability to inspect and redirect ongoing work remains a central design challenge. We present…
articles.abstract: AI agents can assist scientific research, but balancing autonomous investigation with scientists' ability to inspect and redirect ongoing work remains a central design challenge. We present DiscoveryAgent, a domain-agnostic, scientist-centric system that combines autonomous investigation with scientist-directed hypothesis steering. Scientists select, refine, or replace hypotheses between research rounds, while audit agents interrogate checkpointed records to trace claims, reproduce analyses, and inform subsequent decisions. Across two predictive modeling tasks, DiscoveryAgent produced the best variable-star classifier among evaluated baselines and, with scientist steering, a protein variant-effect predictor surpassed by only one of 106 ProteinGym baselines. We develop a rigorous checkpointing system that enables highly capable audit agents, a scalable form of oversight for agentic research. Audit agents autonomously identify errors at higher rates than previous AI scientist agents, and scientists collaborating with audit agents identify 14x more valid errors versus scientists performing manual review. In three case studies led by domain experts across physical science, social science, and life science, we developed a multimodal photometric-redshift estimator that resolves complementary failures of images and photometry, achieving 0.971 AUROC for low-redshift classification; documented an 83% rise in Florida homeowners-insurance premiums from 2013 to 2023, with a growing, regressive burden; and identified CD4+ T-cell relay genes, which both receive and exert broad transcriptional regulation, enriched for autoimmune disease associations. Together, these results show how autonomous research can expand scientists' empirical reach while centering their authority over research direction and their ability to understand and challenge the evidence.

articles.title: Honest Brokers in AI Regulation: How Public Comments Introduce Evidence to Regulators
articles.summary: The regulation of Artificial Intelligence is susceptible to various forms of capture by industry actors that hold undue influence over the policymaking process, due in part to their information…
articles.abstract: The regulation of Artificial Intelligence is susceptible to various forms of capture by industry actors that hold undue influence over the policymaking process, due in part to their information advantage in developing these technologies. In the following paper, we investigate the roles of public commenters in providing evidence to potential regulation in the USA. We build a corpus of 40 potential regulations, and 2,664 public comments submitted by a variety of stakeholders. We computationally process these texts to extract evidence meant to inform regulators, in the form of formal citations and informal references. We find significant differences in the type and amount of evidence supplied: Holding comment length constant, business commenters introduce altogether less evidence, and government, university, and civil society commenters provide significantly more research and legal sources. The publication status of cited research is nearly evenly split, with preprints and peer-reviewed articles being introduced by commenters of all types. We further explore patterns of self-citation and find that while it is prevalent amongst all groups, a small cluster of organizations account for over half of all self-citations in our corpus. Our findings complicate a narrative that public comments alone are means to information capture. We interpret these results in terms of the role that commenters attempt to play in the policymaking process-being either an Issue Advocate or an Honest Broker. These findings on the supply of evidence in public comments shed light on an often overlooked form of policymaking that has implications for how and through what sources information is made accessible to regulators of AI.

articles.title: SLED: Sensor SLicing from Edge to Datacenter
articles.summary: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial…
articles.abstract: Modern sensing systems generate large volumes of heterogeneous data streams from multiple sensor modalities, increasing reliance on datacenters for computation, artificial intelligence/superintelligence (AI/SI) inference, and AI/SI training. Each sensor stream may have different network and compute requirements depending on its type and data volume. However, current wireless systems typically allocate resources at the device level, leading to contention among co-located sensor streams, where bulk data transfers may starve latency-critical telemetry. To this end, this paper introduces Sensor Slicing (SL). SL provides deterministic, medium access control (MAC)-level isolation for individual sensors within a single user equipment (UE) in open radio access networks (O-RAN). Using agentic coding techniques, SL is implemented in two O-RAN-compliant packages, reducing development time by 400 times (2 h 40 min [OCUDU] vs. 6.5 weeks [OAI]), 228-fold fewer human prompts (4 vs. 913), and less than half the tokens (0.64B vs. 1.43B). An associated end-to-end framework, SLED, is implemented to establish per-sensor radio and network isolation across edge, campus, and remote high-performance computing (HPC) tiers. Over-the-air wireless experiments demonstrate that while conventional network slicing causes critical delays to increase more than 2,300-fold under high traffic load, SLED maintains stable latency. Scaling evaluations on the two RAN stacks show that throughput remains within 0.9% and 1.4% of expected allocations even as the number of sensor slices increases. The results demonstrate that SLED preserves latency-critical telemetry while effectively utilizing resources across the sensor-to-HPC pipeline. The SLED software and evaluation datasets are publicly available at https://github.com/UNL-CPN-Lab/SLED-Sensor-SLicing-from-Edge-to-Datacenter.

articles.title: DNeo: Your Parallel Draft Model Needs Better Target Feature Encoding
articles.summary: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference…
articles.abstract: Speculative-diffusion decoding uses a small parallel drafter model to generate b draft tokens in one forward pass, which then undergo parallel verification via a larger target model. Faster inference can be achieved when multiple draft tokens pass verification simultaneously. Recent parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark) improve draft quality by conditioning on rich features computed by the target, through a mechanism known as feature encoding. However, standard feature encoding mechanisms have three limitations: (1) they are lossy, applying encoding projections that are destructive to the underlying target feature-space via a discovered effect known as residual mixing, (2) they are memory-less, with no record of previously processed proposals, and (3) they utilize features sampled uniformly from across the target layers, omitting important hidden states. To address these issues, we propose Mixture-of-Features Attention (MoFA), a lightweight feature-encoding approach equipped with a working memory that encodes previously rejected proposals. Leveraging MoFA, rejection memory, and a set of further enhancements, including 2-tap causal convolutions, prefix-only cross-attention, and non-uniform target layer selection, the final architecture, DNeo, achieves 1.3x faster generation speed than SoTA (DFlash-2) without impacting drafter footprint or generation quality. DNeo marks a new state of the art in high quality, fast LLM inference.

articles.title: Domain-Tuned Diffusion Super-Resolution for 4K Facial Asset Maps
articles.summary: Physically based facial assets require 4K albedo and displacement maps for cinematic close-ups, yet generative pipelines commonly produce them at only 1K. Naively applying photographic…
articles.abstract: Physically based facial assets require 4K albedo and displacement maps for cinematic close-ups, yet generative pipelines commonly produce them at only 1K. Naively applying photographic super-resolution is a poor fit: facial UV maps have domain-specific statistics, and displacement is a scalar height field whose errors directly distort geometry. We present a domain-tuned diffusion upscaler for 4x (1024 to 4096) facial asset super-resolution. Starting from a bilinearly upsampled map, we adapt a frozen SDXL backbone per modality with lightweight LoRA modules, while a Tile ControlNet preserves input structure as the diffusion prior restores pore- and wrinkle-scale detail. On held-out maps, our method produces sharper, more faithful detail than bilinear and off-the-shelf GAN and diffusion super-resolvers, reducing albedo LPIPS from 0.21 to 0.08 while avoiding misplaced or excessive displacement relief. These results show that lightweight domain adaptation can produce render-ready 4K facial asset maps without a custom super-resolution architecture.

articles.title: Language Models Can Rewrite Their Own Weights
articles.summary: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A…
articles.abstract: Language models are trained once, frozen and deployed: improving one again takes another training run, and a prompt, a scaffold or extra computation at inference is gone once the task ends. A frontier model has been shown to edit the weights of a much smaller one. We ask whether a model can rewrite its own weights to make itself better, and find that it can, by its own reasoning, with no gradients and no training; we call this self-rewriting. Given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, a 27B model diagnoses its failure and edits the weights behind it. It surpasses itself: its own edit makes it 6.6 points more accurate on 490 problems it never saw, in a test fixed in advance, and another session's edit also makes it significantly better. It keeps getting better: it submits an edit only when its own tests support it, each edit replacing the last, and over its first eight such sessions its accuracy only rises. Unlike test-time scaling, the gain persists in its weights and adds no cost per answer; unlike training, it needs no pre- or post-training infrastructure, only an open model and hours on one GPU. It repairs a damaged copy of itself: it locates the corrupted matrix and rewrites it with values of its own, never reading the undamaged weights; found on text math problems alone, the repair lifts the copy on six image benchmarks it never saw from 7% to 70% accuracy, 83% of the undamaged model's. And the ability emerges with scale: across four sizes of one family, the 2B model makes no edit and the 4B and 9B models break themselves; only the 27B model works on itself as a human would, comparing its hidden states on answers that finish and on answers that run out of tokens, weakening the direction that separates them. Like a human, a model need not separate training from inference; improving a language model may come to take a conversation rather than a training run.

articles.title: FaceRiff: Data-Efficient Unified Text-to-3D Face Asset Synthesis via Geometric Conditioning
articles.summary: High-resolution facial datasets with consistent UV-mapped geometry, albedo, and physically based displacement are scarce, yet such assets are essential for photorealistic digital-human rendering.…
articles.abstract: High-resolution facial datasets with consistent UV-mapped geometry, albedo, and physically based displacement are scarce, yet such assets are essential for photorealistic digital-human rendering. Existing 3D face generation methods are often slow, single-modality, or require large specialized datasets. Meanwhile, large image diffusion models encode strong facial priors but do not natively produce lighting-independent textures, pore-scale displacement, or UV-aligned geometry. We present FaceRiff, a unified, data- and parameter-efficient framework for generating complete 3D face assets (mesh, albedo, and displacement) directly from text in a shared UV space. FaceRiff adapts a pretrained SDXL backbone with task-specific LoRA adapters and uses UV normal maps as geometric conditioning: per-instance normals guide albedo and displacement synthesis, while a dataset-mean normal provides a canonical spatial anchor for mesh generation. Using only 2,049 scans from approximately 350 identities and training on a single GPU, FaceRiff updates less than 3% of the backbone parameters per task and produces render-ready 3D face assets without per-instance optimization. Compared with FaceG2E and DreamFace, FaceRiff produces greater per-prompt diversity while preserving prompt alignment and fixed-topology UV consistency, and additionally generates lighting-independent albedo suitable for PBR relighting and pore-scale displacement absent from prior text-driven baselines. A blind study with 45 industry professionals shows that FaceRiff achieves substantially higher perceived realism than DreamFace, approaching that of real captures. Overall, FaceRiff demonstrates that pretrained diffusion priors can be adapted to unified 3D face asset synthesis under limited data.

articles.title: AR-WAM: efficient streaming world-action modeling for autonomous driving
articles.summary: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and…
articles.abstract: Autonomous driving requires anticipating how traffic will evolve while responding quickly to new observations. Video foundation models offer the first ability, but repeated history encoding and iterative video generation make them costly to use for driving. We present AR-WAM, an efficient streaming world-action model that combines autoregressive temporal modeling with single-pass future conditioning. Because its video backbone is causal, AR-WAM updates its visual context incrementally, reusing past computation and conditioning future prediction on observed motion. We further hypothesize that future features computed from recent observations can improve generalization in dynamic traffic without iterative video generation. AR-WAM therefore obtains these features in one forward pass and uses them to condition trajectory generation, and reinforcement learning then improves the policy through direct optimization of driving rewards. With a single front camera, AR-WAM achieves 91.5 PDMS after supervised training and 94.0 after reinforcement learning on NAVSIM-v1, outperforming the compared strong end-to-end world-action models. In a dynamic setting of continuous driving, supervised AR-WAM keeps its visual history across decisions and outperforms strong world-action baselines.

articles.title: EmbedGym: Letting Coding Agents Develop and Debug Embedded Firmware Without Physical Hardware
articles.summary: Modern coding agents perform well on general software benchmarks because they can run code and unit tests in a closed loop. Embedded firmware development, however, breaks this loop: a program that…
articles.abstract: Modern coding agents perform well on general software benchmarks because they can run code and unit tests in a closed loop. Embedded firmware development, however, breaks this loop: a program that compiles can still fail on real hardware due to pin polarity, bus protocol, timing, or networking bugs that an agent at a text terminal cannot observe. Existing embedded coding agents either skip hardware execution, drive GPIO-only simulators with multi-second delays, or test on physical boards in a static environment. In this paper, we present EmbedGym, an interactive virtual hardware environment that lets coding agents develop and debug embedded firmware without physical hardware. EmbedGym uses instruction-level microcontroller unit (MCU) emulators to execute the same binary that would be flashed onto a physical board, connects them to 41 peripheral models, an analog circuit simulator, and virtual WiFi/Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) endpoints, and exposes an interface for agents to change sensor inputs, press buttons, and inspect hardware states. On top of it, we build EmbedGym-Bench, which consists of 598 tasks across 6 MCU-framework pairs graded by hidden timed test vectors, using a five-stage multi-agent workflow that synthesizes peripheral models and tasks from datasheets and driver libraries. We expose EmbedGym to a coding agent at three levels and evaluate eight models over more than 14K trajectories. Even when compilation succeeds 99.7% of the time, 19.9% of compiled firmwares fail at runtime (up to 73% on individual targets). In contrast, interactive hardware testing in EmbedGym increases pass rates across models by +4.9% to +14.7% (up to +31% on individual targets). Our results also show that an agent with EmbedGym outperforms prior embedded agent frameworks, and lightweight models with EmbedGym match frontier models without it at 30-70x lower cost.

articles.title: Auditors Struggle to Catch Sabotage In End-to-End Transcripts of AI Safety Research
articles.summary: As AI systems are increasingly used to automate AI R&D, misaligned systems could sabotage research intended to improve model safety and alignment. To stress-test defenses against such sabotage, we…
articles.abstract: As AI systems are increasingly used to automate AI R&D, misaligned systems could sabotage research intended to improve model safety and alignment. To stress-test defenses against such sabotage, we use a human expert as a proxy saboteur on AI safety research. We conduct a red-team/blue-team game where a human researcher runs AI safety experiments from scratch and auditors try to tell which were sabotaged and how. Given access to the full research transcript and the ability to run experiments, human auditors mostly fail to distinguish sabotaged from benign research: they achieve an AUROC of 0.59, not significantly better than chance, and fully identify the specific sabotage in only 17% of cases. Despite not being allowed to run experiments, the best frontier models outperform human auditors (Fable 5.1: AUROC 0.73, 32% full identification) within noise and weaker models perform comparably. When the saboteur chooses which experiments are attacked, rather than being required to sabotage every question given, sabotage identification drops further. Our results suggest that research sabotage by expert-level agents is difficult to detect with current auditing methods and provide a new setting for studying research sabotage.

articles.title: How Much of SAR Vehicle Recognition Is the Vehicle? Background Shortcuts, Angle Gaps and Partial Libraries on MSTAR and ATRNet-STAR
articles.summary: Deep networks score near 99% on the MSTAR vehicle benchmark, and the newer ATRNet-STAR benchmark was built to be harder. We ask how much of these scores comes from the vehicle itself.
articles.abstract: Deep networks score near 99% on the MSTAR vehicle benchmark, and the newer ATRNet-STAR benchmark was built to be harder. We ask how much of these scores comes from the vehicle itself. With a modern network (ConvNeXt-Small, 3 seeds) we first reproduce the known MSTAR result: with the central 96x96 pixels zeroed out, accuracy is still 73.3% (chance 10%). The same shortcut is present in ATRNet-STAR, which was collected across several scenes: with the vehicle removed, accuracy is 63.3% on the 40-class SOC split (chance 2.5%). Under the official scene-change split, the background stops helping and starts hurting. Accuracy is 22.8% on full chips and 30.8% when only the vehicle is shown. A SAR foundation model, SARATR-X, leans on the background more than ConvNeXt does (+4 to +6 points with the vehicle removed, in every seed) and does not solve the scene change. We then hold the amount of training data fixed and vary the depression angles used for training. Accuracy is set mainly by the gap to the nearest training angle: 57% at 15 degrees, 39% at 30 degrees and 26% at 45 degrees. Adding more training angles does not help. Finally, when most classes have training images at the test angle and a few do not, the missing classes do worse than when no class has them: 9.0% instead of 22.4% at a 45-degree gap. Most of their images are assigned to known classes. We recommend reporting background-only and target-only controls, and the angle gap, next to any accuracy figure. Code is public.

articles.title: TUSI: A Citation-Grounded Graph-Based Benchmark
articles.summary: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in Persian law remains challenging because benchmarks lack realism, grounding, and coverage of legal reasoning. Existing resources are either…
articles.abstract: Evaluating retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) systems in Persian law remains challenging because benchmarks lack realism, grounding, and coverage of legal reasoning. Existing resources are either synthetically generated from statutory texts, lacking natural information needs, or derived from informal legal question--answer sources without explicit linkage to authoritative legal documents, making them unsuitable for rigorous evaluation of grounded legal reasoning. To address this gap, we introduce TUSI-Bench, a structured Persian legal benchmark designed for the evaluation of RAG-based systems. TUSI-Bench is built upon a multi-layered legal knowledge framework containing 7,261 legal articles and integrating codified statutes, legal commentaries, doctrinal writings, and Supreme Court unification rulings. We also construct a legal knowledge graph linking articles and concepts for structure-aware retrieval. Based on this foundation, TUSI-Bench provides two complementary evaluation tasks: (i) TUSI-QA, an open-ended question answering benchmark containing 1,999 questions that requires grounded responses with explicit legal citations, and (ii) TUSI-Bar, a multiple-choice benchmark containing approximately 500 four-option questions derived from Iranian Bar examination questions. Furthermore, we propose a graph-based retrieval baseline that leverages relational structure within the legal knowledge graph. Experimental results demonstrate that incorporating graph-based relations improves retrieval recall by up to 8 percentage points compared to standard baselines, highlighting the importance of structured legal representations for RAG systems. The proposed benchmark provides a standardized resource for evaluating grounded legal reasoning in Persian and enables future research on structured legal intelligence.

articles.title: ARC-2: Continuous Compliance Through Delta Management
articles.summary: ARC 1 introduced a three-layer governance architecture for autonomous systems comprising model safety validation, cognitive certification (CRAB), and operational authorization (LEA). However, it did…
articles.abstract: ARC 1 introduced a three-layer governance architecture for autonomous systems comprising model safety validation, cognitive certification (CRAB), and operational authorization (LEA). However, it did not address how compliance should be maintained after deployment. This paper introduces Delta Management, a continuous governance framework that measures deviations between a system's current operational state and its certified baseline, defined as a region rather than a fixed point. Compliance is assessed through continuous monitoring instead of static certification. Four extensions are proposed. First, CRAB evaluation incorporates the worst verified behavioral deviations, with isolated outliers quarantined pending confirmation to prevent unjustified restrictions. Second, a layered trigger taxonomy distinguishes hard safety violations, critical single-dimension failures, correlated multi-system degradation, and risk-weighted composite indicators, each triggering proportionate responses. Third, a graduated safe transition protocol separates withdrawal of operational authorization from physical shutdown, consistent with established safety standards and EU AI Act requirements. Fourth, environmental delta is introduced as a distinct baseline validity condition: environmental drift beyond the certified Operational Design Domain (ODD) triggers recertification or ODD revision rather than automatic authority contraction. Together, these extensions transform ARC from a deployment-time certification architecture into a continuous framework for monitoring, evaluating, and enforcing compliance throughout the operational lifecycle of autonomous systems. The framework addresses the continuous compliance obligations established by EU AI Act Article 72(2).

articles.title: Evaluating the Evaluation of Music Generation Models with Generative Psychometrics
articles.summary: Subjective user studies are one of the major methods for evaluating music generation models. However, subjective evaluation protocols vary widely and are rarely specified in enough detail to be…
articles.abstract: Subjective user studies are one of the major methods for evaluating music generation models. However, subjective evaluation protocols vary widely and are rarely specified in enough detail to be reproduced, hindering comparison across studies. In this paper, we map subjective evaluation methods in ISMIR music generation papers from 2020-2025 and apply generative psychometrics to assess the stability of their items. We extract 284 items from the papers' methodological descriptions, using an LLM and manual validation to standardize them. We represent these items as contextual embeddings and apply Unique Variable Analysis to remove redundant, locally dependent items and Bootstrap Exploratory Graph Analysis to estimate their latent dimensions. Results show the network converges onto a taxonomy of six stable quality dimensions: Rhythm, Melody, Audio, Composition, Structure, and Lyrics, pointing to a unified methodology for conducting user studies to evaluate music generation models.

articles.title: SimAI: Mechanistic User Simulation through Psychological Network Models
articles.summary: Realistic user simulation enables the study of human interactions when direct experimentation is costly or potentially harmful. However, existing simulators largely overlook the psychological…
articles.abstract: Realistic user simulation enables the study of human interactions when direct experimentation is costly or potentially harmful. However, existing simulators largely overlook the psychological mechanisms that drive user behavior. We introduce SimAI, a framework for mechanistic user simulation that models how psychological factors interact to shape user responses. To overcome the challenge of supervising open-ended behavior, we propose a graph reconstruction objective that provides graph-level rewards based on how well simulated conversations reflect the underlying psychological relationships. To support this approach, we construct PSYCHE, a dataset of 18,576 profile-network pairs derived from 516 psychotherapy cases. Automatic evaluations show that SimAI achieves greater simulation and behavioral diversity than existing patient simulators while maintaining strong profile alignment. In an interactive study with 30 mental-health professionals and trainees, SimAI receives the highest average ratings for conversational authenticity, realistic help-seeking behavior, and clinical training utility. Beyond simulation quality, SimAI enables realistic clinical training and uncovers safety failures in prolonged AI interactions with vulnerable users. Code is available at https://github.com/behavioral-data/ANGEL-UserSim.

articles.title: Can Coding Agents Write and Transpile Unit Tests
articles.summary: Coding assistants built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a staple of modern software development, increasingly trusted to execute workflows and modernize code end-to-end. Much of this…
articles.abstract: Coding assistants built on Large Language Models (LLMs) have become a staple of modern software development, increasingly trusted to execute workflows and modernize code end-to-end. Much of this trust rests on passing tests, which are often written by the coding agents themselves. In this work, we examine the ability of these agents to both write reliable tests and translate them between programming languages. We benchmark three popular coding agents, each evaluated with a native frontier model and high reasoning effort. Verifying across a broad suite of metrics, we find that coding agents far exceed human written suites on traditional measures of coverage. This advantage, however, is uneven: agent test quality degrades sharply with project size, and much of the advantage lies in a greater number of written tests. We also show that agentic test translation---while seemingly strong in aggregate---remains inconsistent and unreliable.

articles.title: Revisiting the Survival of Agent-Attributed Code: How Measurement Choices Decide the Verdict
articles.summary: Studies of how long code from AI coding agents survives after it is merged reach conflicting verdicts: agent code is reported to be retained longer than human code, about as long, or modified sooner.…
articles.abstract: Studies of how long code from AI coding agents survives after it is merged reach conflicting verdicts: agent code is reported to be retained longer than human code, about as long, or modified sooner. Each study makes defensible measurement choices, but how much these choices decide the verdict is unknown. We revisit the survival of agent-attributed code in our earlier study: 854,139 lines that 2,802 merged pull requests (PRs) added to 215 repositories of the AIDev dataset. We vary nine measurement choices in five research questions and build a specification curve of 88 survival analyses, tested under three variance estimators, several observation windows, and permuted labels. For code from human-supervised agents, mostly GitHub Copilot, the choices change the size of the effect but not its direction. For code from the fully-autonomous agent Devin, they decide the verdict. Across repositories, 15 of 22 specifications report it modified sooner when lines are treated as independent, but only 3 when standard errors are clustered by repository, no more than permuted labels produce.
